entries.lesson_core_move: Convert a cosine A cos(omega t + phi) into the phasor A angle phi, preserving amplitude and phase for same-frequency phasor addition.

sections.lesson_title: Phasor Representation of a Cosine
sections.section_title: Introduction to Phasor Representation of a Cosine

blocks.text: A phasor is the magnitude-angle version of a cosine. Use $A\cos(\omega t+\phi) \mapsto A\angle\phi$ when the cosine will be handled through same-frequency phasor addition. The amplitude stays $A$, the phase shift becomes the angle, and the shared angular frequency $\omega$ stays separate.
The simplest base case is $A\cos(\omega t)$, which has zero phase. Its phasor is $A\angle 0$, so a cosine with no phase shift becomes a phasor with angle $0$.

For $A\cos(\omega t+\phi)$, keep the amplitude unchanged and carry the phase shift into the phasor angle. The mapping preserves the information needed for later addition: the phasor stores the amplitude and phase, not the time variable.

Keep $\omega$ outside the phasor value. That separation matters later because same-frequency cosines are added only after they have the same $\omega$, and the phasors then carry only the magnitude and angle.

sections.lesson_title: Phasor Representation of a Cosine
sections.section_title: Writing a Zero-Phase Cosine as a Phasor

example_content.example_prompt: Convert $6\cos(\omega t)$ into phasor form.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a cosine with no phase shift: $A\cos(\omega t)$. Use the phasor convention that keeps the amplitude and converts the phase to an angle, so the base form is $A\angle 0$.

For this example, the amplitude is $6$ and the phase shift is $0$, so the cosine $6\cos(\omega t)$ becomes the phasor $6\angle 0$. Nothing changes except the notation: the time-varying cosine is now written as a magnitude-angle pair.
Keep the shared angular frequency $\omega$ outside the phasor. The phasor stores only amplitude and phase, which is the form needed later when same-frequency terms are added.

sections.lesson_title: Phasor Representation of a Cosine
sections.section_title: Writing a Positive-Phase Cosine as a Phasor

example_content.example_prompt: Convert $4\cos(\omega t+\pi/3)$ into phasor form.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a cosine with a positive phase shift: $4\cos(\omega t+\pi/3)$. Use the phasor rule $A\cos(\omega t+\phi) \mapsto A\angle\phi$, so the amplitude stays $A$ and the phase becomes the angle.

For this example, the amplitude is $4$ and the phase shift is $\pi/3$, so the cosine $4\cos(\omega t+\pi/3)$ becomes the phasor $4\angle\pi/3$. The positive sign stays in the angle; it does not change the amplitude.
Keep the shared angular frequency $\omega$ outside the phasor. The phasor stores only magnitude and phase, which is the format needed later when same-frequency terms are added.

sections.lesson_title: Phasor Representation of a Cosine
sections.section_title: Writing a Negative-Phase Cosine as a Phasor

example_content.example_prompt: Convert $10\cos(\omega t-\pi/6)$ into phasor form.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a cosine with a negative phase shift: $10\cos(\omega t-\pi/6)$. Use the phasor rule $A\cos(\omega t+\phi) \mapsto A\angle\phi$, so the amplitude stays $A$ and the phase stays attached to the angle.

For this example, the amplitude is $10$ and the phase shift is $-\pi/6$, so the cosine $10\cos(\omega t-\pi/6)$ becomes the phasor $10\angle-\pi/6$. The minus sign stays in the angle; it does not move to the amplitude.
Keep the shared angular frequency $\omega$ outside the phasor. The phasor stores only magnitude and phase, which is the format needed later when same-frequency terms are added.

sections.lesson_title: Phasor Representation of a Cosine
sections.section_title: Separating the Shared Angular Frequency from the Phasor

example_content.example_prompt: Convert $12\cos(\omega_0 t-\pi/4)$ into phasor form and keep $\omega_0$ separate from the phasor value.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a cosine with shared angular frequency $\omega_0$ and phase shift $-\pi/4$: $12\cos(\omega_0 t-\pi/4)$. Use the phasor rule $A\cos(\omega t+\phi) \mapsto A\angle\phi$, and keep the angular frequency outside the phasor.

For this example, the amplitude is $12$ and the phase shift is $-\pi/4$, so the cosine $12\cos(\omega_0 t-\pi/4)$ becomes the phasor $12\angle-\pi/4$. The symbol $\omega_0$ stays separate because the phasor holds only magnitude and phase.
That separation matters later when same-frequency cosines are added. The phasor carries the amplitude and phase, while the shared angular frequency is handled outside the phasor value.

entries.lesson_core_move: Add same-frequency cosines by recognizing their common angular frequency, converting each cosine to its phasor, and summing the phasors as complex quantities.

sections.lesson_title: Adding Same-Frequency Cosines
sections.section_title: Introduction to Adding Same-Frequency Cosines

blocks.text: When two cosine terms share the same angular frequency, do not add them directly in the time domain. Treat the shared $\omega$ as the cue that the terms belong to one phasor-addition problem, then convert each cosine to a phasor and add the phasors as complex quantities.

Start with the base case $A\cos(\omega t)+B\cos(\omega t)$. The shared $\omega$ tells you that both terms use the same frequency tag, so each cosine becomes a zero-phase phasor before anything is added.

The same rule works for phase-shifted cosines such as $A_1\cos(\omega t+\phi_1)+A_2\cos(\omega t+\phi_2)$. Keep the common $\omega$ outside the phasor value, and convert the amplitudes and phases into $A_1\angle\phi_1$ and $A_2\angle\phi_2$.

After conversion, add the phasors as ordinary complex quantities. The frequency tag $\omega$ does not get added; it is only the shared label that tells you the cosines are comparable at the same frequency.

This step is just the setup: recognize the shared $\omega$, rewrite each cosine as $A\angle\phi$, and write the complex sum cleanly. Later steps will make the phasor sum more explicit, but this lesson starts with the recognition-and-setup move.

sections.lesson_title: Adding Same-Frequency Cosines
sections.section_title: Recognizing a Common Angular Frequency

example_content.example_prompt: In $4\cos(5t+\pi/6)+7\cos(5t-\pi/3)$, identify the shared angular frequency and decide whether the terms can be combined as same-frequency phasors.

explanation_blocks.text: Read the coefficient of $t$ in each cosine argument. The first term has $5t+\pi/6$ and the second term has $5t-\pi/3$, so both cosines carry the same angular frequency.
Because both terms use the same $\omega$, the pair is eligible for phasor addition. The amplitudes $4$ and $7$ and the phases $\pi/6$ and $-\pi/3$ do not change that decision.
State the result explicitly: the shared angular frequency is $\omega=5$, so these two cosines can be treated as one phasor-addition problem.
This recognition step does not convert anything yet; it only confirms that the later phasor conversion is valid because the frequency is common.

sections.lesson_title: Adding Same-Frequency Cosines
sections.section_title: Converting Each Cosine to a Phasor

example_content.example_prompt: Convert $4\cos(5t+\pi/6)+7\cos(5t-\pi/3)$ into a phasor-sum expression.

explanation_blocks.text: Because the two cosines already share $\omega=5$, this step is just a notation conversion. Read the first term's amplitude and phase as $4$ and $\pi/6$, then read the second term's amplitude and phase as $7$ and $-\pi/3$.
Write the first cosine as $4\angle\pi/6$. The amplitude stays with the phasor, and the phase becomes the angle.
Write the second cosine as $7\angle-\pi/3$ and keep the shared frequency tag $5$ outside the phasors. That keeps the notation frequency-preserving.
The phasor-sum form is $4\angle\pi/6 + 7\angle-\pi/3$. Nothing has been added yet; this step only converts each cosine cleanly so the next step can combine the phasors.

sections.lesson_title: Adding Same-Frequency Cosines
sections.section_title: Forming the Resultant Phasor Sum

example_content.example_prompt: Form the resultant phasor sum for $5\cos(3t)+5\cos(3t-\pi/2)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the shared angular frequency $\omega=3$, so the two terms can be handled as one phasor-addition problem. The converted phasors are already visible from the cosine data: the first term has amplitude $5$ and phase $0$, and the second term has amplitude $5$ and phase $-\pi/2$.

Write the result as the phasor sum $5\angle 0 + 5\angle(-\pi/2)$. The plus sign is ordinary complex addition, so the two phasors are combined directly instead of being turned back into time-domain cosines.
The resultant expression stays in phasor form for now. That keeps the shared frequency $3$ attached to the sum and leaves rectangular or polar simplification for the next step.

sections.lesson_title: Adding Same-Frequency Cosines
sections.section_title: Adding More Than Two Same-Frequency Cosine Phasors

example_content.example_prompt: Convert $2\cos(7t)+3\cos(7t+\pi/4)+4\cos(7t-\pi/3)$ into one phasor-sum expression.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the shared angular frequency $\omega=7$ in all three cosine terms. That means the whole expression is one phasor-addition problem, and each cosine should be carried into phasor form without dropping any term.

Convert the zero-phase term to $2\angle 0$, the positive-phase term to $3\angle\pi/4$, and the negative-phase term to $4\angle-\pi/3$. Each amplitude stays attached to its own phasor, and the shared frequency label remains $7$.

Write the full phasor-sum expression as $2\angle 0 + 3\angle(\pi/4) + 4\angle(-\pi/3)$. The plus signs mean ordinary complex addition, and the expression stays in phasor form rather than being collapsed into rectangular coordinates yet.
The result shows the rule scales unchanged from two terms to three: keep the common $\omega$, convert every cosine to its phasor, and add all of them together as a single complex sum.

entries.lesson_title: Rectangular Form of a Phasor Sum
entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the rectangular-form phasor sum for same-frequency cosines by resolving each phasor into real and imaginary components and adding corresponding components.

sections.lesson_title: Rectangular Form of a Phasor Sum
sections.section_title: Introduction to Rectangular Form of a Phasor Sum

blocks.text: From the earlier phasor representation, keep the common $\omega$ fixed and rewrite each same-frequency phasor in rectangular form. A rectangular phasor has the form $a+jb$, where $a$ is the real part and $b$ is the imaginary part.
So if $X_1 = a_1 + jb_1$ and $X_2 = a_2 + jb_2$, the phasor sum is formed componentwise: add the real parts together and add the imaginary parts together.
The same bookkeeping works for three or more phasors. Collect every real part into one total and every imaginary part into another total, and keep the result rectangular for now.

That is the rule the later examples will reuse: same $\omega$, rectangular components, and componentwise addition. The next step can turn this rectangular sum into polar form, but this section stops at the rectangular result.

sections.lesson_title: Rectangular Form of a Phasor Sum
sections.section_title: Adding Axis-Aligned Phasor Components

example_content.example_prompt: Add the phasors $3 + j0$ and $0 + j5$ and write the result in rectangular form.

explanation_blocks.text: These phasors are already axis-aligned, so the rectangular parts are visible immediately. Write them as $X_1 = 3 + j0$ and $X_2 = 0 + j5$.
Now add the real parts and the imaginary parts separately. The real-part total is $3 + 0$, and the imaginary-part total is $0 + 5$.
So the rectangular-form phasor sum is $3 + j5$.

sections.lesson_title: Rectangular Form of a Phasor Sum
sections.section_title: Resolving Two Cosine Phasors into Rectangular Components

example_content.example_prompt: Find the rectangular-form phasor sum of $4\cos(\omega t + 60^\circ)$ and $6\cos(\omega t - 30^\circ)$.

explanation_blocks.text: Because the two cosines share the same $\omega$, convert each one to a phasor first. Write $X_1 = 4\angle 60^\circ$ and $X_2 = 6\angle -30^\circ$.
Now resolve the real and imaginary parts of each phasor. The first phasor becomes $X_1 = 2 + j2\sqrt{3}$, and the second becomes $X_2 = 3\sqrt{3} - j3$.
So the rectangular-form phasor sum is $(2 + 3\sqrt{3}) + j(2\sqrt{3} - 3)$.

sections.lesson_title: Rectangular Form of a Phasor Sum
sections.section_title: Adding Phasors with Negative Rectangular Components

example_content.example_prompt: Add the phasors $(-4 + j3)$ and $(1 - j6)$ and write the result in rectangular form.

explanation_blocks.text: These phasors are already in rectangular form, so preserve the signs and add the real parts and imaginary parts separately. Call them $X_1 = -4 + j3$ and $X_2 = 1 - j6$.
Now add the signed real parts and the signed imaginary parts. The real-part total is $-4 + 1 = -3$, and the imaginary-part total is $3 + (-6) = -3$.
So the rectangular-form sum is $-3 - j3$.

sections.lesson_title: Rectangular Form of a Phasor Sum
sections.section_title: Adding More Than Two Same-Frequency Phasors in Rectangular Form

example_content.example_prompt: Add $4 + j0$, $-1 + j3$, and $2 - j2$ and write the result in rectangular form.

explanation_blocks.text: All three terms are already in rectangular form, so keep the signs and add the real parts and imaginary parts across the whole list. Label them $X_1 = 4 + j0$, $X_2 = -1 + j3$, and $X_3 = 2 - j2$.
Group the real parts as $4 + (-1) + 2$ and the imaginary parts as $0 + 3 + (-2)$. Then add each group separately.
So the rectangular-form sum is $5 + j1$.

entries.lesson_title: Polar Form of a Phasor Sum
entries.lesson_core_move: Convert a rectangular phasor sum into polar magnitude-angle form so the resultant sinusoid's amplitude and phase can be read from the phasor.

sections.lesson_title: Polar Form of a Phasor Sum
sections.section_title: Introduction to Polar Form of a Phasor Sum

blocks.text: After a same-frequency cosine sum has been collected into a rectangular phasor $Z = a + jb$, the next step is to write it in polar magnitude-angle form so the corresponding sinusoid's amplitude and phase can be read directly from the phasor.

The magnitude is the length of the phasor vector in the complex plane, so compute it from the rectangular components with the Pythagorean formula. That magnitude is the amplitude of the resultant sinusoid.

To get the angle, first read a reference angle from the component ratio, then place that angle in the correct quadrant using the signs of $a$ and $b$. Writing $\theta = \operatorname{atan2}(b, a)$ keeps those two steps together.

For the clean base case $Z = 4 + 3j$, the phasor lies in the first quadrant, so the magnitude is $5$ and the angle is the first-quadrant angle with $\tan\theta = 3/4$. The polar form is $Z = |Z|\angle\theta$, and later worked examples will vary only the signs and quadrant choice.

sections.lesson_title: Polar Form of a Phasor Sum
sections.section_title: Computing the Magnitude of a Rectangular Phasor Sum

example_content.example_prompt: Find the magnitude of the rectangular phasor sum $Z = (3 + j4) + (1 + j2)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a rectangular phasor sum, so first add the real parts and the imaginary parts separately. That gives the single rectangular phasor whose magnitude we want.
Now the phasor is in rectangular form with $a = 4$ and $b = 6$. Apply the Euclidean norm $|Z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ to get the magnitude.
So the magnitude of the rectangular phasor sum is $|Z| = 2\sqrt{13}$. That is the value you carry forward when the phasor is written in polar form.

sections.lesson_title: Polar Form of a Phasor Sum
sections.section_title: Computing the Reference Angle of a Rectangular Phasor Sum

example_content.example_prompt: From the sum $Z = -4 + 3j$, compute the reference angle.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a rectangular phasor with mixed signs, so isolate the acute reference angle from the component ratio. For this step, use absolute values so the sign pattern does not change the angle itself.
Here $a = -4$ and $b = 3$, so the acute ratio is $|b|/|a| = 3/4$. Apply the reference-angle rule $\theta_{\text{ref}} = \tan^{-1}(|b|/|a|)$ to get the angle.
So the reference angle is $\theta_{\text{ref}} = \tan^{-1}(3/4)$. That acute angle is the value you carry into the later quadrant step.

sections.lesson_title: Polar Form of a Phasor Sum
sections.section_title: Choosing the Correct Quadrant for the Phasor Angle

example_content.example_prompt: For the rectangular phasor $Z = -5 + 12j$, find the quadrant-adjusted phase angle.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a rectangular phasor whose signs already tell you the quadrant. First find the acute reference angle from the component ratio, then apply the quadrant rule to turn it into the principal phase angle.
Here $a = -5$ and $b = 12$, so the reference angle is based on the absolute values: $\theta_{\text{ref}} = \tan^{-1}(12/5)$. Because $a < 0$ and $b > 0$, the phasor lies in quadrant II.
Quadrant II means the principal angle is the supplement of the reference angle, so subtract it from $\pi$. That gives the final phase angle for the phasor.
So the quadrant-adjusted phase angle is $\theta = \pi - \tan^{-1}(12/5)$. The workflow is always the same: read the signs, get the reference angle, then apply the quadrant correction.

sections.lesson_title: Polar Form of a Phasor Sum
sections.section_title: Writing the Polar Phasor Sum and Reading Its Magnitude and Angle

example_content.example_prompt: Convert the rectangular phasor sum $Z = 1 - \sqrt{3}j$ into polar form and state the corresponding magnitude and phase.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a rectangular phasor sum, so the job is to convert it into polar form and read off both the magnitude and the phase. Use the rectangular components to get the magnitude first, then use the sign pattern to place the angle in the correct quadrant.
Here $a = 1$ and $b = -\sqrt{3}$. The magnitude is $|Z| = \sqrt{1^2 + (\sqrt{3})^2} = 2$, and the absolute-value ratio gives the reference angle $\theta_{\text{ref}} = \tan^{-1}(\sqrt{3}/1) = \pi/3$.
Because $a > 0$ and $b < 0$, the phasor lies in quadrant IV, so the principal phase angle is the negative of the reference angle. That gives the final polar form.
So the phasor is $Z = 2ngle -\pi/3$. The magnitude $2$ is the sinusoid's amplitude, and the angle $-\pi/3$ is its phase.

entries.lesson_title: Converting a Phasor Sum Back to a Sinusoid
entries.lesson_core_move: Convert a polar phasor sum back into a single same-frequency sinusoid by mapping magnitude to amplitude and angle to phase at the common angular frequency.

sections.lesson_title: Converting a Phasor Sum Back to a Sinusoid
sections.section_title: Introduction to Converting a Phasor Sum Back to a Sinusoid

blocks.text: When a polar phasor sum is written as $A\angle\phi$ at a common angular frequency $\omega_0$, the conversion target is one same-frequency cosine. Read the magnitude as amplitude, read the angle as phase, and keep the angular frequency unchanged.

The base case shows the defaults: magnitude $1$ becomes amplitude $1$, and angle $0$ becomes zero phase. Nothing changes in the frequency term, so the same $\omega_0$ stays outside the phasor-to-cosine mapping.

So the rule is simple: magnitude becomes amplitude, angle becomes phase, and the shared $\omega_0$ stays fixed. The next examples in this topic will keep that same mapping while isolating amplitude, phase, frequency, and then the full conversion.

sections.lesson_title: Converting a Phasor Sum Back to a Sinusoid
sections.section_title: Identifying the Sinusoid Amplitude from Phasor Magnitude

example_content.example_prompt: A phasor sum is $7\angle 25^\circ$ at common angular frequency $\omega_0$. Identify the amplitude of the equivalent same-frequency cosine.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue in this step is the phasor magnitude. Here the phasor sum is $7\angle 25^\circ$ at common angular frequency $\omega_0$, so the number to read first is the $7$.
Match that magnitude to the amplitude of the equivalent same-frequency cosine. The angle $25^\circ$ stays in the background for this step, and the common angular frequency $\omega_0$ is unchanged.
So the amplitude is $7$. This example isolates only the magnitude-to-amplitude mapping; the phase and full cosine form are handled in later steps.

sections.lesson_title: Converting a Phasor Sum Back to a Sinusoid
sections.section_title: Identifying the Sinusoid Phase from Phasor Angle

example_content.example_prompt: A phasor sum is $4\angle -\pi/3$ at common angular frequency $\omega_0$. Identify the phase of the equivalent same-frequency cosine.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue in this step is the phasor angle. Here the phasor sum is $4\angle -\pi/3$ at common angular frequency $\omega_0$, so the angle to read is $-\pi/3$.
Match that angle to the phase of the equivalent same-frequency cosine. Preserve the sign exactly, and keep the amplitude $4$ and the common angular frequency $\omega_0$ unchanged for this step.
So the phase is $-\pi/3$. This example isolates only the angle-to-phase mapping; the full cosine form is handled later.

sections.lesson_title: Converting a Phasor Sum Back to a Sinusoid
sections.section_title: Preserving the Common Angular Frequency in the Sinusoid

example_content.example_prompt: A phasor sum is $3\angle \pi/6$ at common angular frequency $\omega_0=4$. Write the matching cosine and keep the frequency exactly as given.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue in this step is the common angular frequency. Here the phasor sum is $3\angle \pi/6$ at common angular frequency $\omega_0=4$, so the frequency term stays fixed at $4$.
Keep that $4$ unchanged in the cosine argument. The magnitude $3$ gives the amplitude and the angle $\pi/6$ gives the phase; this step only checks that the frequency is preserved exactly as stated.
So the matching cosine is $x(t)=3\cos(4t+\pi/6)$. No new frequency appears, and no existing frequency term is changed.

sections.lesson_title: Converting a Phasor Sum Back to a Sinusoid
sections.section_title: Writing the Complete Cosine from a Polar Phasor Sum

example_content.example_prompt: A phasor sum is $9\angle -\pi/4$ at common angular frequency $\omega_0=2$. Write the complete equivalent cosine.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue in this step is the complete conversion. Read the magnitude as the amplitude, read the angle as the phase, and carry the common angular frequency through unchanged.
Here the phasor sum is $9\angle -\pi/4$ at common angular frequency $\omega_0=2$, so the amplitude is $9$, the phase is $-\pi/4$, and the frequency term stays $2t$.
So the complete equivalent cosine is $x(t)=9\cos(2t-\pi/4)$. This final example combines the three isolated mappings from the earlier steps into one answer.

entries.lesson_title: Amplitude-Phase Form of a Sinusoidal Sum
entries.lesson_core_move: Express a same-frequency sinusoidal sum in amplitude-phase form by adding component phasors and converting the resultant magnitude and angle into the combined amplitude and phase.

sections.lesson_title: Amplitude-Phase Form of a Sinusoidal Sum
sections.section_title: Introduction to Amplitude-Phase Form of a Sinusoidal Sum

blocks.text: A same-frequency sinusoidal sum should be read as a single cosine of the form $A\cos(\omega t+\phi)$ after the component phasors are added. This lesson is about turning the sum into that one cosine and reading off the combined amplitude and phase.
Do not add the amplitudes and phases directly. Keep the shared $\omega$ fixed, convert each cosine to its phasor, and use phasor addition as the only combination step.
The phasor bridge is the same for each term: a cosine becomes a phasor with the same magnitude and angle, and those phasors add as vectors.

In the base two-cosine case, the resultant phasor gives the answer: its magnitude becomes the new amplitude and its angle becomes the new phase. Later examples will keep the same angular frequency and add only one new wrinkle to this phasor-to-cosine loop.
So the reusable rule is simple: hold the common $\omega$ fixed, add the component phasors, and read the resultant magnitude and angle as the single cosine's amplitude and phase.

sections.lesson_title: Amplitude-Phase Form of a Sinusoidal Sum
sections.section_title: Combining Two Same-Frequency Cosines into One Cosine

example_content.example_prompt: Combine $4\cos(8t+\pi/3)$ and $2\cos(8t-\pi/6)$ into one cosine in amplitude-phase form.

explanation_blocks.text: Both terms share the same angular frequency $8$, so the right move is to convert each cosine to a phasor, add the phasors, and then read the resultant magnitude and angle back as one cosine.
Convert each cosine to a phasor first. Then add the phasors in rectangular form so the shared frequency stays fixed and the arithmetic stays component-wise.

The resultant phasor has magnitude $2\sqrt{5}$, and its angle is the quadrant-I angle of $(2+\sqrt{3})+j(2\sqrt{3}-1)$. That magnitude and angle are the new amplitude and phase of the combined cosine.
So the complete loop is: keep the common $\omega$ unchanged, add the component phasors, and convert the resultant magnitude and angle back into one cosine.

sections.lesson_title: Amplitude-Phase Form of a Sinusoidal Sum
sections.section_title: Finding the Resultant Amplitude and Phase from Component Phasors

example_content.example_prompt: The component phasors are $3+j4$ and $2-j1$. Find the amplitude and phase of the combined sinusoid.

explanation_blocks.text: The component phasors are already in rectangular form, so the first move is to add the real parts and the imaginary parts separately.
That rectangular result is the resultant phasor. Because both parts are positive, the angle is the quadrant-I angle of the point $(5,3)$.

So the combined sinusoid has amplitude $\sqrt{34}$ and phase $\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{3}{5}\right)$ at the shared angular frequency. Later examples can reuse the same rectangular-addition workflow and only change the component values.

sections.lesson_title: Amplitude-Phase Form of a Sinusoidal Sum
sections.section_title: Keeping the Correct Quadrant for the Resultant Phase

example_content.example_prompt: Convert the phasor sum $-2+j3$ into the amplitude-phase form of the corresponding cosine.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the rectangular phasor $-2+j3$. Treat it as a vector: first find its magnitude, then choose the phase from the signs of the real and imaginary parts.
Use the absolute values to get the reference angle. That gives $\theta_{\text{ref}} = \tan^{-1}(3/2)$, but this is not the final phase yet.

So the phasor is $\sqrt{13}\angle\left(\pi - \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)\right)$, and the corresponding cosine is $x(t)=\sqrt{13}\cos\left(\omega t+\pi-\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)\right)$.

sections.lesson_title: Amplitude-Phase Form of a Sinusoidal Sum
sections.section_title: Combining More Than Two Same-Frequency Cosines

example_content.example_prompt: Combine $2\cos(6t)+2\cos(6t+\pi/3)+2\cos(6t+2\pi/3)$ into one cosine in amplitude-phase form.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is three same-frequency cosines at angular frequency $6$. Put each term into a phasor, add the phasors, and then convert the result back to amplitude-phase form.
Convert each phasor to rectangular form so the real and imaginary parts combine directly. Here the $1$ and $-1$ real parts cancel, which makes the sum easy to read.
Now read off the magnitude and phase from the rectangular sum. Since $Z$ is in Quadrant I, the principal angle is the correct angle.
So the three cosines combine to one cosine at the same frequency $6$, with amplitude $4$ and phase $\pi/3$.
